items.title: 2nd Circ. Says No Surprises Act Limits Private Right Of Action - Law360
items.reason: This is a Second Circuit court decision directly interpreting the No Surprises Act's private right of action—a core litigation development that affects enforcement mechanisms and revenue-cycle operations.
items.summary: The Second Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the No Surprises Act limits the scope of private right of action available to patients suing for balance-billing violations. This decision clarifies what legal remedies patients can pursue directly under the federal law and has implications for how healthcare providers and insurers defend against balance-billing claims. The ruling affects enforcement dynamics for the balance-billing protections established under the No Surprises Act and may influence litigation strategy across states, particularly in the Second Circuit's jurisdiction covering New York, Connecticut, and Vermont.

items.title: New IDR portal sign-ups open for No Surprises Act disputes - techtarget.com
items.reason: The item directly addresses the Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process, a core operational component of No Surprises Act implementation, though it appears to be an operational/procedural update rather than litigation or rulemaking.
items.summary: A new IDR portal has opened for sign-ups to process Independent Dispute Resolution disputes under the No Surprises Act. The portal enables parties to register and participate in the federal IDR process, which resolves balance-billing disputes when in-network and out-of-network providers cannot agree on payment amounts. This development affects healthcare providers, payers, and third-party administrators managing surprise billing claims under the Act's framework. For revenue-cycle teams, access to this portal is critical for submitting and tracking IDR cases, which represent an alternative dispute-resolution mechanism to traditional appeals for out-of-network billing disputes.

items.title: Lawsuit Says UnitedHealth Used AI With a 90% Error Rate to Deny Care - Yahoo
items.reason: This reports a lawsuit against UnitedHealthcare (a major payer) alleging use of a flawed AI system to deny claims, which is a core example of payer litigation involving claims-denial practices.
items.summary: A lawsuit alleges that UnitedHealthcare used an artificial intelligence system with a 90% error rate to deny patient care and insurance claims. The suit challenges the payer's automated claims-denial practices, which directly impacts provider reimbursement and patient access to covered services. This litigation exemplifies claims-denial enforcement actions against major payers and raises material concerns for revenue-cycle teams regarding claim rejections, appeals processes, and the need to document denials based on flawed algorithmic decisions.
